 Buffet Drawing Templates 
 Mangia has a certain way of setting up buffets to ensure efficient serving.  This form 
 outlays the general setting for a buffet.  While some items will vary on each buffet the 
 general theory remains.  Use your judgment to set up the buffet onsite in accordance to 
 the Mangia way shown here.  Pizza buffets follow the same layout as shown below. 
 Notes: 
 For hot items, in chafers, the veggie items go first (closest to plates), the starch items go 
 second, the proteins go third. We put less expensive items first.  Rice would go before 
 mac n cheese.  Chicken would go before tri tip. 
 Veggies example - veggie mix, carrots, green beans, etc.  Starch example - mac n 
 cheese, potatoes, rice, etc.  Protein example - chicken, pork, beef, etc. 
 For most buffets we will have three hot items, a salad, a bread, and a butter.  If you 
 have more hots or more colds set them up using the same process above.  You can run 
 chafers over into the second table as needed. If you have cold sides like potato salad, 
 mac salad, place BEFORE the salad. 
 Arrange items to fill in the table.  We do not want open table space.  Say you only have 
 2 hots - set up just one buffet table (not two).  Or if you must do two tables you can 
 rotate chafers 90 degrees to fill up space. 
 UTENSILS 
 What to use: 
 We want to use the best utensil to efficiently serve food in a timely manner.  In addition we want 
 to be mindful of the serving size. 
 Check with lead: 
 Verify the serving utensil plan with leads for BOH to make sure you are on the same page. Use 
 the back of this page to write the utensil plan down! 
 Examples: 
 Standard Tongs - Pulled Pork, Tri Tip, Shredded Beef, Chicken 
 Small Tongs - Bread, Relish, Pickles 
 Spatulas - Salmon, Pizza 
 Spoons - Mac and Cheese, Mashed Potato, Cubed Chicken 
 Slotted Spoons - Veggies, Black Beans, Pinto Beans 
 Tablespoons - BBQ Sauce, Mayo, Olives

Ops Final Lock — Training Resource 
 Role:  Operations  Owner of this process:  Ops team  Purpose:  Move an event from Sales Lock 
 → Ops Final Lock → Print Ready  Source of truth:  Total  Party Planner (TPP)  Companion 
 documents:  Ops Final Lock  checklist,  Event Forms One  Print  (both in Google Drive) 
 Welcome 
 Your job inside this process is not to play detective. Sales has already sold the event, confirmed 
 the menu, and locked in who, what, when, where. By the time an event hits your queue, the 
 heavy lifting on the client side is done. 
 Your job is to make sure the event is  actually ready  to go out the door  . You are the last set of 
 eyes before the warehouse starts packing and the chefs start cooking. You are protecting the 
 brand, the margin, and the guest experience by making sure nothing slips through. 
 If you do this right, the team in the field shows up prepared, the client never sees a seam, and 
 Mangia looks exactly the way it's supposed to look. If you miss something here, it shows up in 
 the field as a missing tent tarp, a wrong linen color, a chef without the right utensils, or a staff 
 member without a call time. Those are expensive mistakes, both in dollars and in reputation. 
 Treat this process like the final QC walk on a luxury product. Every event leaves the building at 
 the Mangia standard, or it doesn't leave. 
 Part 1: What You Need to Know Before You Start 
 The three-phase flow 
 Every event at Mangia moves through three gates: 
 1.  Sales Lock.  Sales finalizes the client, menu, guest  count, timing, and billing. They mark 
 the event Sales Lock in TPP. At this moment, the event hands off to Ops. 
 2.  Ops Final Lock.  This is your gate. You review everything  in TPP line by line against the 
 Ops Final Lock  checklist. You clean up the packlist,  confirm vehicles, confirm timing, 
 confirm equipment, and resolve anything ambiguous. When you're done, you mark the 
 event status as Final.

3.  Print Ready.  Once Ops Final Lock is complete, you print all the documents, build the 
 physical binder, export to Nowsta, and mark the event Ready on the Event Tracker. The 
 warehouse can now pack. The chefs can now prep. The field team can now be 
 scheduled. 
 The TPP calendar color code 
 Open TPP and go to your  Week View  (not Month — too  much noise). You will see events 
 color-coded: 
 -  Light green  → Sales Lock. Ready for  you  to do Ops  Final Lock. 
 -  Light blue  → In between. Actively being worked on,  not yet final. 
 -  Dark green  → Final. Done, printed, ready. 
 If you're doing your Ops Final Lock block, you're looking for light green events. Those are your 
 queue. 
 Why pen and paper matter 
 When you sit down to do an Ops Final Lock, you print the checklist and work through it line by 
 line with a pen. We do not scan the checklist on a screen. Humans skim screens and miss 
 things. The physical act of checking off each line forces you to actually verify each line. This is 
 non-negotiable. 
 Part 2: Setting Up Your Workstation 
 Before you open the first event, get your whole environment ready. Fumbling between tabs 
 mid-review is how details get missed. Set up once, then work clean. 
 Pull up these windows, in this order, ready to go: 
 1.  Total Party Planner (TPP)  — center screen. Your source  of truth. 
 2.  Ops Final Lock checklist  — printed on paper, next  to your keyboard. 
 3.  Event Forms One Print  — the one-print checklist that  lives with the event binder. 
 Google Drive. 
 4.  Event Tracker  — Google Drive. Where you log NLT, vehicle,  truck/trailer assignment. 
 5.  Google Drive  — open and ready. 
 6.  Dropbox  — open to the event's folder. Venue drawings,  photos, and assets live here. 
 7.  Slack  — open on the event's dedicated channel. 
 8.  Nowsta  — our scheduling software. You'll need it at  the end to export.

If you are on a single screen, you'll rotate through these. On a dual monitor, split them so TPP is 
 always visible. 
 The reason we insist on this setup: when the Ops Final Lock checklist says  Check Dropbox for 
 rentals  , you should be one click from the answer,  not three minutes of hunting. Speed and 
 accuracy come from preparation. 
 Part 3: The Ops Final Lock, Line by Line 
 Open the event in TPP. Work through the  Ops Final  Lock  checklist in the same order as the 
 document. The sections below match the checklist headers exactly. 
 Section 1: INFO 
 What you verify: 
 -  Service style (C.O.S. / B.H. / P.C. / D.O. / Plate / Fam / Vend) 
 -  Guest count 
 How:  Click the  Info  tab inside TPP. Cross-check the  service style against the checklist options. 
 The service style determines what equipment you'll pack, what vehicle you'll use, what kit you'll 
 pull. Mark it on the paper checklist. Verify the guest count against what sales locked in. 
 Red flag logic:  If anything in this section is blank,  missing, or inconsistent, stop. Do not 
 continue forward. Raise the flag with the salesperson or the sales office. An event that wasn't 
 finished by sales cannot be finished by ops. Do not paper over their gap. 
 Section 2: EVENT MENU 
 What you verify: 
 -  Menu items are in the correct order 
 -  All quantities are correct 
 -  No items are marked  ***  or  ... 
 -  Menu Production is checked for notes 
 -  All items are in the correct category for the service style 
 How:  Open the menu inside the event. Our house order  is:  mains first, then sides, then 
 dessert/place settings last.  Pizza → bread → salad  → drinks → dessert is a correct flow. 
 Dessert before the mains is not.

Walk the quantities against the guest count. If the guest count is 130 and you see an item priced 
 at 500, something broke. Raise the flag. 
 The  ***  and  ...  markers mean an item is an  empty shell  — no description, no proposal note, 
 no pack list attachment, no recipe. If you push an event through with a  ***  or  ...  item, the 
 warehouse packs nothing for it and the kitchen orders nothing for it. This is one of the 
 highest-impact errors you can catch at this stage. 
 "Menu Production checked for notes" means you read the line notes on each item. Notes tell 
 you things like  "French fries served in cone, not  tray"  — the culinary team needs to pack the 
 cone. Or  "Caesar dressing on the side, add extra bowl."  If the note exists, the team has to know. 
 For category: a cook-on-site event should have cook-on-site items, not drop-off items. If the 
 categories don't match the service style, something got miscoded upstream. Flag it. 
 Section 3: TIMELINE 
 What you verify: 
 -  Staff scheduled ON time 
 -  NLT (No Later Than) entered 
 -  Staff arrival onsite time entered 
 -  Serve times are correct (  3 hours prior to service  for full-service, 1.5 hours prior for 
 limited-service  ) 
 How:  TPP is our source of truth for timing. Even though  Nowsta also holds the schedule, we 
 enter the timing here first, so the field team and ops team can look at one place and get the real 
 answer. 
 The math: 
 -  Start from the event serve time (say, 11:30 AM buffet open). 
 -  Back out 3 hours for full-service arrival (so staff onsite at 8:30 AM). 
 -  Back out travel time to get  departure from shop  (if  it's a 30-minute drive, they leave shop 
 at 8:00 AM). 
 -  Back out 1 hour to load (staff scheduled ON at 7:00 AM). 
 If you don't know the drive time, check Google Maps. Do not estimate. For larger events with 
 more equipment or more vehicles, give the load window more than one hour. 
 The  staff OFF time  gets similar treatment. Typical:  1 hour after event end for cleanup and 
 reload, plus travel time back, plus unload at shop. Build the schedule so the crew isn't still on 
 the clock figuring things out at 9 PM when sales said the event ends at 6.

Section 4: SETUP NOTES 
 What you verify: 
 -  Notes are checked and "edited to amplify" 
 -  Linen color (black / white / ivory) is called out for tables 
 -  Linen color for baskets / trays is called out 
 -  Setup diagrams — is one needed? Is it in Dropbox? 
 How:  The notes field is the  North Star for the field  team.  By the time they arrive on site, they 
 should be able to look at the notes and understand the who, what, when, where, why of the 
 event without calling you. 
 Sales writes the first version of these notes. You  edit to amplify  — this is the phrase you'll hear 
 often. It means: fill the gaps, kill the redundancy, add the detail the field team needs. 
 Examples of what belongs here: 
 -  "5 gluten-free meals" 
 -  "Plan B for rain — guests inside building under tent" 
 -  "Black linens for tables" 
 -  "Rustic kit: wood platters, white marble bowls, hammered serving ware" 
 -  "Setup diagram: Dropbox > green number 1" 
 As you read through,  capture any detail that will  affect packing  , because the packlist is 
 coming up next and you'll need this information in your head. Some ops people keep a scratch 
 pad on the side for this. Do what works for you. 
 If the event needs a setup diagram (plated meals, multi-station events, complex venues), verify 
 it exists in Dropbox. Then take a screen grab or export and  post it into the event's Slack 
 channel.  The field team should not have to go digging  through Dropbox on their phones the 
 morning of. 
 Section 5: PACKLIST 
 This is the most important section in the entire process.  Most of what can go wrong at an 
 event traces back to a packlist error. Slow down here. Don't rush. 
 What you verify: 
 -  Notes added on servingware type 
 -  Quantities checked — flag anything unusually high 
 -  X -  items removed

-  Equivalent  items packed and assigned 
 -  Equipment needed added (handwashing, tent, flooring, etc.) 
 -  Plasticware in Other Inventory Items (if applicable) 
 -  Vehicles assigned, equipment assigned 
 How: 
 Open the packlist inside the event. Keep it sorted  by category  as your default view. Category 
 sort groups items the way the warehouse is physically organized, so the packer is walking the 
 building in logical order. You can sort alphabetically if you're hunting one item, but always return 
 to category view. 
 Also, select the show all blue button and load entire list. This allows you to see the association if 
 the pack list item. 
 Add notes on servingware type.  If the notes said "rustic  kit with wood platters and white 
 marble bowls," go down the packlist and tag the serving items accordingly: serving board → 
 wood board; small bowl → white marble bowl. If the note applies to three of the same item, you 
 don't have to write it three times — TPP prints it in one section. 
 Check quantities.  Look for anomalies. 500 linens on  a 130-person event is wrong. 10 chafers 
 on a plated dinner for 40 is wrong. A running mental check: does this quantity make sense for 
 the guest count and service style? 
 Watch for doubles.  Sometimes the same item gets associated  twice. Unpack the duplicate. 
 Every duplicated rolled utensil at $1.50 × 100 = real money wasted. Clean inventory discipline 
 here is how margin stays healthy. 
 X -  items.  These are placeholder or excluded items.  Remove them before print. If you see  X - 
 and something beside it like  X - Equivalent needed  ,  that means we need the equivalent 
 item packed (e.g.,  X - Wood-fired pizza oven equivalent  → we need a pizzeria 
 trailer). Don't just delete blind. Read before you cut. 
 Equipment check.  Handwashing, tent, flooring. Even  if these are usually on the standard 
 packlist, verify every time. Use the  Pack List Report  view (separate screen) and Ctrl-F / Cmd-F 
 for the word — "tent", "handwashing", "tarp". If it's missing, add it: 
 Event → Manage → search item → verify correct variant (e.g., for a 10x20 tent on 
 soft surface, you need two 10x10 tarp equivalents) → set quantity → Add to Pack 
 List. 
 Then go back to the packlist and confirm the item is now there.  Trust but verify. Always.

Plasticware.  If plasticware is in play, make sure it's in Other Inventory Items. 
 Vehicles and equipment assigned.  Check the  Event Tracker  in Google Drive. Each event row 
 should have: 
 -  Event date 
 -  Event number 
 -  NLT 
 -  Event type / name 
 -  Truck assignment 
 -  Trailer assignment (if applicable) 
 This sheet is displayed in the ops warehouse. The whole team sees it. No one person should be 
 the bottleneck on "which truck is going to which event." 
 Section 6: EQUIP 
 What you verify: 
 -  Dropbox checked for rentals file 
 -  Decor from Good Shuffle verified 
 -  Coordinating serving items match service type 
 How:  Most rental coordination is now done by sales  on the front end — they drop the rustic kit 
 into the Good Shuffle order and print it themselves. Your job is to  verify it's there  , not to create 
 it. 
 If the event notes say something like  "Event Rents  providing X, Y, Z"  , that's your cue to check 
 Dropbox for the Event Rents file. If the notes don't mention rentals, rentals are probably not 
 involved — but still look. 
 If decor is missing (kit not added to Good Shuffle, for example), ping sales in Slack on the event 
 channel: 
 "Can you add Rustic Kit to GU Law event?" 
 Keep the loop tight. Don't escalate without giving the owner a chance to fix it first. 
 Coordinating serving items: if we're doing a plated meal, do we have trays and tray jacks? If 
 we're doing stations, do we have the station equipment? This is the judgment layer.

Section 7: BEV (Beverage) 
 Usually blank unless we're doing bar service. If there are beverage items flagged for attention, 
 address them. If not, move on. 
 Section 8: BAR 
 If there's a bar, there's a whole separate training and process. For most events this section is a 
 one-line confirm. 
 Section 9: WRAP UP 
 What you do: 
 1.  Mark event status to Final.  Click Final in TPP. The  event turns dark green on the 
 calendar. Enter today's date as the Final Approval Date. 
 2.  Export to Nowsta.  Click the Nowsta button in TPP.  It exports the shift structure to 
 Nowsta with call times, but without the actual staff assigned yet. Confirmation message: 
 "Your event has been exported." 
 3.  Mark "Binder — Ready to Build"  on the Event Tracker  so the warehouse knows it's 
 coming. 
 At this point, the Ops Final Lock itself is done. Now you build the binder. 
 Part 4: Binder Creation 
 Every event leaves the shop with a physical binder. The binder is the field team's playbook. If 
 the internet goes down, the phone dies, or the chef walks in cold, the binder tells them 
 everything they need to know. 
 Binder color code 
 -  Red binder  → cooked on site (full service) 
 -  Green binder  → limited service, cook at kitchen 
 -  Blue clipboard  → drop-offs 
 -  Blue half-inch binder  → bar service 
 Grab the right color. Don't improvise.

Binder prep 
 -  Wet erase marker → label the white spine with the  event number  . Make it as large and 
 spaced-out as possible so the warehouse can read it from across the room. Example: 
 6423  . 
 -  Pre-stock: pens, dividers, Sharpie, chalk marker, regular pen, business cards, injury 
 report sheet, phone number sheet, accident reporting form. These go in every binder, 
 every time. Ops restocks the bulk pile. 
 What to print 
 One copy per document unless otherwise noted.  Print  everything before you assemble. 
 1.  Worksheet  — TPP > Event > Worksheet. This particular  event called for  2 copies 
 (check the event — some call for 2). Print > Ops Printer >  2  > Collate on. 
 2.  Event Menu  — TPP > Reports > Event Menu. The front-of-house  team's at-a-glance for 
 what's being served. 
 3.  Pack List (by Item Type)  — This is the  reference packlist  .  Shows every item built out 
 by dish. For example, a Farmer's Market Pizza lists spatula, pizza boxes, dough, pesto, 
 semolina — everything that makes the pizza. When this prints,  the ops person writes 
 REF  in the header  so the packer knows this is not  the one they pack off of. This is the 
 cross-reference. 
 4.  Pack List (by Category)  — This is the  packing packlist  .  Change the report parameters 
 to  Category  . Same data, grouped by warehouse category  so the packer walks the 
 building efficiently. This is the one they check off as they pack. 
 5.  Event Forms One Print  — The multi-form document in  Google Drive. See Part 5 below 
 — you fill parts of this out  before  printing. 
 6.  Nowsta Timesheet PDF  — In Nowsta, find the event →  Timesheet PDF. Prints team 
 call times and phone numbers. 
 7.  Good Shuffle Pull Sheet  — Sales sends this to the  ops printer. If they haven't, prompt 
 them on Slack:  "Send Good Shuffle to Ops Printer when  complete." 
 For remote venues, also print: 
 -  Venue map (Google Maps screenshot) 
 -  Setup diagram / venue drawings from Dropbox 
 When in doubt, print more, not less. In the field without signal, paper wins.

Part 5: Filling Out the Event Forms One Print 
 The Event Forms One Print is a multi-section document. Some sections you fill  before printing 
 (because they're ops decisions). Some sections are filled  in the field  by the event lead. Know 
 which is which. 
 Sections YOU fill before printing 
 Event Task Breakdown (Tab 1):  Walk through each line  and mark Y or N based on the event's 
 actual scope. Examples: 
 -  Servingware:  Plasticware / Rented / Client Provided  — underline the right one. 
 -  Take rentals with us: Y/N 
 -  Leave rentals onsite: Y/N 
 -  Setup guest tables/chairs: Y/N 
 -  Setting tables with flatware/china: Y/N 
 -  Fill water goblets: Y/N 
 -  Setup buffet tables: Y/N 
 -  Setup tables for appetizers: Y/N 
 -  Setup table for beverages: Y/N (note: if beverages go on the buffet table, mark N here) 
 -  Stationary apps / Apps on their own table / Apps using main buffet / Pass apps 
 -  Set out beverage dispensers: Y/N 
 -  Serving buffet / Self-serve buffet 
 -  Bus after dinner / Full bus 
 -  Dessert: setup / cut / serve / coffee bar 
 The rule of thumb:  we always serve buffets unless  indicated otherwise.  We do not 
 self-serve. We bus after dinner but we do not full-bus unless the contract says so. 
 If a line doesn't apply (e.g., no appetizers), mark N. If a line is a no-op for the whole event (e.g., 
 no dessert), N everything in that block. 
 This form is a quick-glance for staff who arrive on site but weren't part of the loadout team. It 
 has to be unambiguous. 
 Sections the FIELD LEAD fills (do not pre-fill) 
 -  Leaving the Shop Checklist  — filled before departing  the commissary 
 -  Event Arrival Checklist  — filled on arrival at the  venue (5 min walkthrough) 
 -  Event Food MUDA  — filled after the event to track  waste 
 -  Bin Organization Sheet  — fill bin numbers before loadout,  circle dirty bins after 
 -  After Event Form  — filled by the event lead immediately  post-event

-  Event Return Checklist  — filled at shop after return 
 -  Event Packing Checklist  — filled by the packer 
 -  Buffet Drawing Template  — use for setup; we have a  standard buffet flow 
 -  Leaving the Event Checklist  — filled before departing  the venue 
 -  Before Takeoff Checklist (BTCL)  — filled by Event  Lead  with  Warehouse Lead before 
 event is marked "ready" on Event Tracker. This one has two signatures. 
 Your job on these sections is to make sure they're  in the binder, printed clean, blank and 
 ready  for the field team to use. 
 The buffet standard (reference) 
 Even though the field team runs the buffet, know the standard so you can spot a weird event: 
 -  Hot items in chafers:  veggies first (closest to plates),  starches second, proteins third. 
 Cheaper items first (rice before mac & cheese, chicken before tri tip). 
 -  Standard buffet:  3 hots, a salad, a bread, a butter. 
 -  Cold sides:  place before the salad. 
 -  Arrangement:  fill the table. No open space. If you  have only 2 hots, use one buffet 
 table, not two. Rotate chafers 90° if needed to fill. 
 Part 6: Assembling the Binder 
 Once everything is printed: 
 1.  Three-hole punch  every document that goes in the binder  rings. 
 2.  Packing dockets  (color-coded sleeves): the packlist  goes in a red sleeve for full-service 
 / cook-on-site, green for limited service / cook at kitchen. Bar and equipment packing 
 have their own sleeves. 
 3.  Packing docket goes to the warehouse shelf  so the  packer can find it. The rest of the 
 documents go into the binder itself. 
 4.  Worksheet  goes in the front cover slip of the binder  (one worksheet, clearly visible from 
 outside). 
 5.  Event number on the spine  in wet erase. 
 6.  Binder goes on the Event Binder Rack. 
 When packing is done 
 -  The packer takes the packlist off the shelf, walks the warehouse, checks each item. 
 -  When done, the packlist goes  into the binder on the  event rack.

-  Someone (Event Lead + Warehouse Lead) runs the  Before Takeoff Checklist  and 
 signs off. 
 -  Event Tracker status → FULLY PACKED → READY. 
 At that point, the loop is closed. The event is fully prepped to ship. 
 Part 7: Communicating as You Go 
 Mangia runs on Slack. The two habits to build day one: 
 One channel per event.  Naming convention:  event-number  event-name  , e.g. 
 6423-GU-Law  . When you find a setup diagram, screen-grab  it and post it in the channel. When 
 you need sales to add a kit to Good Shuffle, ask in the channel. Keep everything in one place so 
 the field team doesn't have to chase. 
 Reply in threads.  When a conversation starts on an  event, keep it threaded. It keeps the main 
 channel clean and the history readable. 
 Part 8: Glossary 
 These are the terms and tools you'll hear on day one. Memorize them. 
 TPP — Total Party Planner.  Our catering management  software. Events, menus, packlists, 
 timelines, client contacts all live here. This is the source of truth. 
 Sales Lock.  The point at which sales has finalized  the event contract, menu, guest count, and 
 timing. Event is ready for ops review. 
 Ops Final Lock.  Your job. The final review from the  ops side before the event is marked Final 
 and goes to production. 
 Final / Print Ready.  The event has passed Ops Final  Lock, all documents are printed, binder is 
 built, Nowsta is exported, warehouse can pack. 
 NLT — No Later Than.  The latest departure time from  the shop for the event. Built backward 
 from serve time. 
 Packlist.  The full list of equipment, servingware,  ingredients, and assets being packed for the 
 event. Two views:  by item type  (reference) and  by  category  (packing).

Worksheet.  The TPP-generated summary sheet for the  event. Goes in the front cover slip of 
 the binder. 
 Event Forms One Print.  The multi-section field operations  document. Lives in Google Drive.

 Part 10: Principles to Work By 
 A few things to hold onto as you grow into this role. 
 Trust but verify.  Sales may have done their job perfectly.  The packlist may look complete. The 
 rentals may already be ordered. Verify anyway. You are the last line. 
 When in doubt, check.  It's always cheaper to double-check  than to ship something missing. A 
 30-second Ctrl-F beats a 6 AM call from a field lead asking where the tarps are. 
 Stay in your silo — but own it fully.  This process  is not the place to reopen menu decisions, 
 renegotiate the contract, or rewrite the client's notes. It is the place to make sure everything that 
 was decided is actually executed correctly. Own the execution. 
 Raise flags early.  If something is broken upstream  (missing info, contradictory notes, 
 star-star-star items), stop, name it, and escalate. Don't paper over it. A broken event caught now 
 is a thousand times cheaper than a broken event caught at the venue. 
 Protect the brand.  Every piece of equipment that goes  out, every minute of timing, every detail 
 on that binder is part of the Mangia experience. You are the final person touching the event 
 before it goes out the door. Treat it like the finished product it is.
